classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the right triangle linking the sphere radius, cylinder radius and half-height, then use the supplied intermediate results to form and differentiate the volume function. Select the positive feasible stationary height, justify its maximum and substitute into a volume ratio; the explicit staged targets make these routine linked procedures.

content.prompt: A cylinder of height $h$ metres is inscribed in a sphere of constant radius $R$ metres.

spec.sourceRegion: Diagram below question 33 at the left
spec.description: Transparent sphere containing a vertical cylinder, with elliptical ends, a central vertical construction line, top radius r, full height h and sphere radius R from the sphere centre to the upper-right rim. Lower-face radial construction lines are retained. Nonsemantic source face shading is omitted under house style.
spec.mathematics: The sphere centre lies halfway between the cylinder end centres. The right triangle has perpendicular lengths r and h/2 and hypotenuse R.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no calculated answers are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the cylinder has radius $r$ metres, show that $r^2=R^2-\frac14h^2$.

answer.worked:
The sphere centre is halfway up the cylinder. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}R^2&=\left(\frac h2\right)^2+r^2\\r^2&=R^2-\frac14h^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by $V=\frac\pi4h(4R^2-h^2)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the cylinder is maximised when $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$.

answer.short: $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$. Since $\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\frac{3\pi h}{2}<0$ for $0<h<2R$, this gives the maximum.
answer.worked:
For a nondegenerate cylinder, $0<h<2R$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dV}{dh}&=\frac\pi4(4R^2-3h^2)\\0&=4R^2-3h^2\\h^2&=\frac{4R^2}{3}\\h&=\sqrt{\frac{4R^2}{3}}\\h&=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R.\end{align*}$$
The positive root is in the domain. Also,
$$\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\frac{6\pi h}{4}<0\qquad(h>0).$$
Thus $V$ is concave down throughout the domain, so its stationary point gives the global maximum.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence show that the ratio of the volume of the sphere to the maximum volume of the cylinder is $\sqrt3:1$.

answer.worked:
At the maximum, $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$ and $h^2=\frac{4R^2}{3}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi r^2h}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi\left(R^2-\frac14h^2\right)\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi\left(R^2-\frac14\frac{4R^2}{3}\right)\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\frac{4\sqrt3}{9}\pi R^3}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Therefore the required ratio is $\sqrt3:1$.
